content: During pregnancy, the rapid growth of the fetus leads to an increased demand for folate due to the proliferation of rapidly dividing cells. If folate intake is insufficient, serum folate levels decrease, which subsequently reduces erythrocyte folate concentrations. This deficiency can result in elevated homocysteine levels and megaloblastic changes in the bone marrow and other tissues with high cellular turnover. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of oral folic acid supplementation, either alone or in combination with other micronutrients, compared to no folic acid (placebo or the same micronutrients without folic acid) during pregnancy. The focus was on its impact on hematological and biochemical parameters during pregnancy and on pregnancy outcomes. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of December 31, 2012. They also reached out to key organizations involved in micronutrient supplementation, including UNICEF Nutrition Section, the World Health Organization (WHO) Maternal and Reproductive Health and Nutrition Divisions, and the National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The review included all randomized, cluster-randomized, and cross-over controlled trials that compared folic acid supplementation (alone or with other micronutrients) to no folic acid during pregnancy. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data, which were subsequently verified for accuracy. A total of 31 trials involving 17,771 pregnant women were included in the review. The findings indicated that folic acid supplementation did not significantly affect pregnancy outcomes such as preterm birth (risk ratio [RR] 1.01, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.73 to 1.38; three studies, 2,959 participants) or stillbirths and neonatal deaths (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.85; three studies, 3,110 participants). However, there was a notable improvement in mean birthweight (mean difference [MD] 135.75 grams, 95% CI 47.85 to 223.68). In contrast, folic acid supplementation did not demonstrate a significant effect on reducing pre-delivery anemia (average RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.10; eight studies, 4,149 participants; random-effects), mean pre-delivery hemoglobin levels (MD -0.03, 95% CI -0.25 to 0.19; 12 studies, 1,806 participants), mean pre-delivery serum folate levels (standardized mean difference [SMD] 2.03, 95% CI 0.80 to 3.27; eight studies, 1,250 participants; random-effects), or mean pre-delivery red cell folate levels (SMD 1.59, 95% CI -0.07 to 3.26; four studies, 427 participants; random-effects). However, a significant reduction in the incidence of megaloblastic anemia was observed with folic acid supplementation (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.38; four studies, 3,839 participants). In conclusion, the review did not find conclusive evidence to support the benefit of folic acid supplementation during pregnancy in improving overall pregnancy outcomes.
